medium.conteudo_html:
I went to a presentation where a guy demoed his “second brain”.

He had taken it out of Claude, and I could see that what he built may not hold a candle to mine technologically. However — commercially his is better. The whole room was full of people who wanted to install it.

And I understood something: the technology does not matter. Nobody cares what the technology is. What matters is that it is easy to install. His onboarding was done very well.

He does not use Mem0 or Zep or any agent memory layer at all. He just uses Obsidian — he uses it to show that he has a pile of files not linked to each other. Orphan files.

So: technology does not matter. What matters is how you position yourself.

I went to check that against numbers, because I happen to hold exactly the measurement that either confirms it or does not.

It confirms it. Painfully.

The number

My public starter kit, live traffic on the day of the post: 2,158 clones from 743 unique sources over fourteen days, against 215 page views from 88 unique visitors. Stars in four months of existence: 15. Forks: 5.

Its neighbour repository: 2,041 clones from 389 unique sources, 282 views from 86 visitors, the same 15 stars, but 17 forks.

Eight times more cloners than humans who even opened the page.

By my own instrument rule that reads as automation rather than interest: clone traffic without page views is almost always robots. So I have a product that machines take in bulk and an audience of eighty-eight visitors.

The man on stage had a full room of live people who wanted to install his.

That is the entire difference, and none of it is technological. I have 17 forks against his zero, and no room.

On Mem0 and Zep he is right, and I measured that too

He noted the presenter uses neither. I went through both companies: roughly 31 people between them, and one of them runs on a graph framework I had already tested against my own corpus back in July and declined — it helped on topic search by about 71 percent and hurt people search.

So I am not avoiding them out of stubbornness, and the overlap with the presenter is not a coincidence. Neither of our decisions was driven by technology. Both were driven by what the thing has to do for the person using it.

Orphan files: the contested point, and the one where I owe an answer

I saw “a pile of files with no links between them” and read it as a weakness. The comments pushed back within minutes: orphans are not a bug, hand-made links do not scale and they rot, and an agent needs a fast fetch of a current chunk rather than a graph to walk.

⚠️ And I have had this exact argument before, under my own post about recall. One commenter argued for a graph over the knowledge base, another argued the graph is unnecessary, and I publicly promised to “answer with numbers”. Those numbers have still not been produced.

Here is what I actually have.

My baseline vault scan in June: 30,724 orphans, 18.3 percent of 167,971 notes. I treated that as a defect and repaired 12,746 files in a single pass. So “an orphan is a defect” is not a theoretical position — there is a linter that catches them daily and names the writer responsible.

But the A/B harness, which compares pure vector retrieval against vector plus one graph hop, says the opposite: a median of 2 new notes per query, and 33 percent of queries with no novelty at all. The usefulness of those new notes has never been measured even once.

So by my own data the commenter is closer to right than I was: the graph adds little, and hand-made links age worse than an index.

Which means the presenter’s pile of unlinked files was not the amateur part of his demo. It was the part I should have been taking notes on.

And the “answer with numbers” I promised in August is still outstanding, with nobody picking it up — including me, three months later, standing in a room judging somebody else’s architecture.

On the call I offered

At the end of the post I said I would be glad to tell anyone how this is built, and that I can do a call.

That one is backed by a live artifact, which is the rare case where a promise in a post does not become a debt: the booking link returns 200 right now and already sits in the link hub under every post. One meeting type, 1-on-1, video.

⛔ With one constraint from my own rules: my exchange order is two-step — ask for the other person’s calendar first, offer mine second. So the link does not go into cold outreach. It goes out immediately in reply to “sounds interesting”, and not before.

What follows, as work rather than as agreement

If “onboarding is what matters” is true, and my own numbers say it is, then my bottleneck is not in the code.

743 cloners against 88 visitors means the person who could install this does not find me, and does not understand it in the first thirty seconds. The presenter does not have better technology. He has a room and an explanation.

The cheapest next check costs less than any build: take those 88 visitors and find out at which step they closed the page. If the answer is “did not understand where to start”, then onboarding really is the whole product — and I will have a measurement of my own rather than somebody else’s observation from somebody else’s stage.

What I take from this

Three things, in order of how much they annoy me.

The first is that I walked into that room as the person with the better engine and walked out as the person with no customers, and both of those were true simultaneously. Technical superiority and commercial irrelevance are not in tension. They were describing different axes the whole time.

The second is that the thing I identified as his weakness — unlinked files — is the thing my own measurement says is fine. I had a defect counter running daily on a problem I have never shown to be a problem for retrieval. The linter is real and the harness disagrees with it, and I had not noticed the two instruments were arguing.

The third is the quiet one. A room full of people is a measurement. So is eighty-eight page views. I had been measuring clones, which is the number that flatters me and describes robots.

medium.resumo: Why the boundary is where the bugs live
medium.conteudo_html:
Why the boundary is where the bugs live

Vue 3.6 lets you mix two rendering engines in one app, and almost every surprising bug shows up exactly where the two meet. Inside a pure Vapor region or a pure Virtual DOM (VDOM) region, things behave the way the docs describe. At the seam between them, three features need extra care: SSR hydration, slots, and KeepAlive.

This guide is written so a beginner can follow it from zero. We start with what Vapor and VDOM actually are, build a small mixed app, and then walk through each gotcha with code, the theory behind it, and a diagram.

TL;DR

  • Vapor Mode compiles a component’s template straight into DOM operations. No virtual nodes, no diffing.
  • A Vapor component inside a normal createApp() app needs vaporInteropPlugin. Every place where a Vapor component sits next to a VDOM component is a boundary.
  • Hydration: both engines must walk the same server HTML in the same order. Mismatched markup or conditional rendering at a boundary is the most common source of hydration warnings.
  • Slots: in Vapor, calling slots.default() actually renders the slot. Never call it just to check whether a slot has content. Use <slot>Fallback</slot> in the template instead.
  • KeepAlive: Vapor templates compile <KeepAlive> into a Vapor-specific version. It can cache VDOM children and the VDOM <KeepAlive> can cache Vapor children, but keys, include/exclude and template refs behave subtly differently at the seam.
  • Keep one rendering mode per region of the screen. Put the boundary above repeated content, never inside a v-for.

Where Vue 3.6 stands today (November 2026)

Vapor Mode is feature-complete but not stable. The 3.6 line entered the release-candidate phase with v3.6.0-rc.1, when the Vue team announced they had finished the intended Vapor feature set. As of this writing, the newest pre-release on the Vue core releases page is v3.6.0-rc.13 (23 October), while the “Latest” stable label sits on v3.5.44 (13 October).

Vue’s own policy treats release candidates as unstable and not meant for production. So the advice for this article is simple: pin an exact RC version in package.json, read the changelog on the minor branch before you bump it, and try Vapor on one screen before planning a migration.

# Pin an exact RC instead of a range
npm install vue@3.6.0-rc.13 --save-exact

A quick note on what you get for free: Vue 3.6 also ships a rewritten reactivity core based on alien-signals. Every 3.6 app benefits from it, whether or not you use Vapor. Vapor itself is a separate, opt-in compilation mode you switch on per component.

Vapor vs VDOM in five minutes

The same .vue file can be compiled two different ways, and the difference decides how updates reach the screen. Understanding this one idea makes every gotcha later in the article easier to follow.

The classic way: Virtual DOM

In normal Vue, your template becomes a render function. Each time reactive state changes, that function runs again and returns a tree of plain JavaScript objects called VNodes (virtual nodes). Vue then compares the new tree with the old one (“diffing” or “patching”) and applies only the differences to the real DOM.

Think of it like redrawing a full sketch of a room every time one chair moves, then comparing the two sketches to find the chair.

The new way: Vapor

In Vapor Mode, the compiler already knows at build time which parts of the template can change. It generates code that creates the DOM once, then attaches a tiny reactive effect to each dynamic spot. When state changes, only the effect tied to that state runs, and it writes directly to the one DOM node it owns.

In the room analogy: someone is assigned to each chair, and only the person watching the moved chair reacts.

Same component, two outputs

Here is a beginner-sized counter. The only difference between the two modes is the vapor attribute.

<!-- Counter.vue -->
<script setup vapor>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2)
</script>
<template>
  <button @click="count++">
    {{ count }} / {{ doubled }}
  </button>
</template>

To understand what changes, look at a simplified sketch of what each compiler produces. These are teaching versions, not the exact output of the Vue compiler.

// VDOM mode (simplified): re-runs on every change, returns new VNodes
function render(ctx) {
  return h('button', { onClick: () => ctx.count++ },
    `${ctx.count} / ${ctx.doubled}`)
}
// Runtime: newTree = render(); patch(oldTree, newTree)
// Vapor mode (simplified): runs once, then fine-grained effects
const t0 = template('<button> </button>')   // static HTML, cloned once

function setup() {
  const button = t0()                        // real DOM node
  const text = button.firstChild
  delegate(button, 'click', () => count.value++)
  renderEffect(() => {                       // re-runs only when count changes
    setText(text, `${count.value} / ${doubled.value}`)
  })
  return button
}

What to notice in the code:

  1. The VDOM render() returns a description of the button. The runtime must compare descriptions to find out what changed.
  2. The Vapor setup() returns the real button. There is nothing to compare later.
  3. renderEffect is the heart of Vapor. It subscribes to exactly the reactive values it reads (count, doubled) and updates exactly one text node.
  4. delegate(...) hints at one behavioural difference we will meet later: Vapor attaches many events through a single listener on document instead of on each element.

Why this matters for the boundary

A VDOM component speaks “VNode”. A Vapor component speaks “real DOM node plus effects”. When one renders the other, an adapter has to translate between the two languages. That adapter is vaporInteropPlugin, and translation is where hydration order, slot functions and KeepAlive caching can disagree.

Opting in, in three ways:

<script setup vapor>   <!-- explicit form -->
<script vapor>         <!-- shorthand for <script setup vapor> -->
<template vapor>       <!-- template-only component in Vapor -->

Only <script setup> and template-only components can be Vapor. Options API components (with data, methods, mounted and so on) always stay VDOM.

Setting up a mixed app (and drawing the boundary on purpose)

There are two ways to start a Vue 3.6 app, and which one you pick decides where your boundaries are.

Option A: an existing VDOM app with some Vapor pages

This is the most common path for real projects: keep the app as it is and convert one performance-sensitive page to Vapor.

// main.js
import { createApp, vaporInteropPlugin } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'        // normal VDOM component

createApp(App)
  .use(vaporInteropPlugin)          // lets VDOM render Vapor children
  .mount('#app')

Without vaporInteropPlugin, a VDOM parent does not know how to mount a Vapor child. With it, props, emitted events and slots are translated in both directions.

Option B: a brand-new, all-Vapor app

// main.js
import { createVaporApp } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'        // <script setup vapor>

createVaporApp(App).mount('#app')

createVaporApp never loads the VDOM runtime, which is where the big bundle-size savings come from. The catch: every component in the tree must be Vapor-compatible. A component written with a render function or JSX is a VDOM component, and many UI libraries still are. You can add .use(vaporInteropPlugin) to a Vapor app to host them, but that pulls the VDOM runtime back in and gives up most of the size benefit.

What exactly is “the boundary”?

A boundary is any parent/child edge where one side is Vapor and the other is VDOM. Every boundary means a translation step: VNodes into DOM blocks, slot functions into slot functions of the other kind, and lifecycle hooks into the other engine’s scheduler.

The Vue team’s own advice in the 3.6 release notes is to keep distinct regions for each rendering mode and avoid mixed nesting as much as possible. In practice, that leads to one rule worth memorising:

Put the boundary above the repeated region, never inside it.

Compare these two versions of a product listing.

<!-- ❌ ProductPage.vue (VDOM): one boundary PER card -->
<script setup>
import ProductCard from './ProductCard.vue'   // Vapor
defineProps(['products'])
</script>

<template>
  <ProductCard v-for="p in products" :key="p.id" :product="p" />
</template>
<!-- ✅ ProductPage.vue (VDOM): ONE boundary for the whole grid -->
<script setup>
import ProductGrid from './ProductGrid.vue'   // Vapor, loops inside
defineProps(['products'])
</script>

<template>
  <ProductGrid :products="products" />
</template>
<!-- ProductGrid.vue -->
<script setup vapor>
import ProductCard from './ProductCard.vue'   // also Vapor
defineProps(['products'])
</script>

<template>
  <ul class="grid">
    <ProductCard v-for="p in products" :key="p.id" :product="p" />
  </ul>
</template>

Why the second version is better:

  1. In the first version, a list of 200 products creates 200 crossings. Each one pays translation cost and is a separate place where hydration or slot handling could go wrong.
  2. In the second version there is exactly one crossing, at <ProductGrid>. Everything below it is pure Vapor, which is the well-tested path.
  3. Debugging gets easier too. If a hydration warning appears, you know there is only one seam to inspect.

Gotcha 1: Hydration across the boundary

Hydration only works when the client walks the server’s HTML in exactly the same order the server wrote it, and at a Vapor/VDOM boundary two different engines share that walk. If either one steps over one node too many or too few, everything after it is misaligned.

First, what is hydration?

With server-side rendering (SSR, for example through Nuxt), the server runs your components and sends ready-made HTML. The user sees content immediately. Then the JavaScript loads and Vue hydrates the page: instead of creating new DOM, it walks the existing nodes and attaches reactivity and event listeners to them.

You can picture a cursor moving through the server HTML. Each component says “the next element is mine”, adopts it, and moves the cursor forward. Fragments (components with several root nodes, v-if branches, v-for lists) are marked in the HTML with comment nodes so the cursor knows where a group starts and ends.

Here is a simplified idea of what the server might send for a VDOM page that contains a Vapor widget. The exact markers are an internal detail and may differ between RCs.

<!-- Simplified illustration, not exact Vue output -->
<main>                     <!-- VDOM: App -->
  <h1>Dashboard</h1>       <!-- VDOM -->
  <!--[-->                 <!-- fragment start -->
  <section class="stats">  <!-- Vapor: StatsPanel adopts this -->
    <span>42</span>
  </section>
  <!--]-->                 <!-- fragment end -->
  <footer>…</footer>        <!-- VDOM again -->
</main>

The Vue team updated the classic hydration code so it recognises Vapor components embedded in VDOM components and skips Vapor-specific anchors, and the interop plugin hydrates in both directions. That machinery works well. The bugs come from our code making the two sides disagree about what the HTML contains.

Gotcha 1a: client-only values inside a Vapor child

<!-- ❌ LiveClock.vue (Vapor) used inside a VDOM SSR page -->
<script setup vapor>
const now = new Date().toLocaleTimeString()
</script>

<template>
  <span class="clock">{{ now }}</span>
</template>

What goes wrong: the server renders “10:00:01”, the browser computes “10:00:03”. The text differs, so Vue reports a mismatch and repairs it. In a pure VDOM tree that is usually just a warning. At a boundary, the repair has to be coordinated by two engines, and a mismatch on a structural node (different element, missing branch) can push the shared cursor out of step, so later siblings are reported as mismatched too.

<!-- ✅ Render a stable value on the server, update after mount -->
<script setup vapor>
import { ref, onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue'

const now = ref('--:--:--')            // same on server and client
let timer
onMounted(() => {                       // runs only in the browser
  const tick = () => (now.value = new Date().toLocaleTimeString())
  tick()
  timer = setInterval(tick, 1000)
})
onUnmounted(() => clearInterval(timer))
</script>
<template>
  <span class="clock">{{ now }}</span>
</template>

Why this works: the first client render produces exactly the server’s text (--:--:--), so hydration adopts the node cleanly. Only after hydration finishes does onMounted run and change the value through a normal reactive update. The same pattern applies to window, localStorage, Math.random(), and anything locale- or timezone-dependent. For ids, use useId() instead of random numbers.

Gotcha 1b: structural branches that depend on the environment

<!-- ❌ Different element structure on server vs client -->
<template vapor>
  <div v-if="typeof window !== 'undefined'">Client</div>
  <p v-else>Server</p>
</template>

This is worse than a text mismatch because the element type differs. The fix is the same idea: render one structure everywhere, and switch after mount with an isMounted ref set in onMounted, or wrap the part in Nuxt's <ClientOnly>.

Gotcha 1c: invalid HTML nesting

<!-- ❌ A <div> inside a <p> is invalid HTML -->
<template>
  <p class="summary">
    <StatsPanel />   <!-- Vapor component whose root is <section> -->
  </p>
</template>

The server happily writes <p><section>…</section></p>. The browser's HTML parser does not: it closes the <p> early and moves <section> out. By the time Vue hydrates, the DOM no longer matches what either engine expects. Use a <div> wrapper, and check your components' root elements before placing them inside <p>, <a>, <button>, or table elements.

Gotcha 1d: async components right at the seam

Async components and async setup() are the most actively fixed area of Vapor hydration in the RC changelogs. Recent entries include advancing hydration past multi-root async components (rc.9), applying hydration strategies to resolved async components (rc.7), and resolving hydration anchors by SSR fragment range ownership (rc.7). If you hit odd behaviour here, two practical habits help:

  • Give components that sit directly on a boundary a single root element. A single root gives the cursor one clear node to adopt.
  • Upgrade to the newest RC before filing a bug. Fixes land weekly.
<!-- ✅ Single-root wrapper around an async Vapor widget -->
<script setup>
import { defineAsyncComponent } from 'vue'
const Chart = defineAsyncComponent(() => import('./RevenueChart.vue')) // Vapor
</script>

<template>
  <div class="chart-slot">   <!-- one stable root at the boundary -->
    <Chart />
  </div>
</template>

Making hydration mismatches easier to debug

In production builds Vue strips detailed mismatch messages. While you test a Vapor rollout, turn them back on in Vite:

// vite.config.js
export default {
  define: {
    __VUE_PROD_HYDRATION_MISMATCH_DETAILS__: 'true'
  }
}

For a value that legitimately differs between server and client (a timestamp you accept), Vue 3.5 added the data-allow-mismatch attribute to silence the warning for that one element. The rc.9 changelog includes a Vapor fix for how allowed mismatches apply v-show, which shows Vapor follows the same mechanism, but test it on your RC.

Gotcha 2: Slots are rendered, not inspected

In Vapor, calling a slot function renders that slot: it creates DOM, starts effects and, during hydration, claims server HTML. Code that calls slots.default() just to peek at its content, a common VDOM habit, therefore has real side effects in Vapor.

A quick slots refresher

A slot lets a parent pass template content into a child. The child decides where it appears with <slot />.

<!-- Parent -->
<BaseCard>
  <template #header>Monthly revenue</template>
  <p>$12,400</p>             <!-- goes to the default slot -->
</BaseCard>

Under the hood, each slot is a function. In VDOM, calling slots.default() returns an array of VNodes, which are just descriptions, so calling it to check something is cheap and harmless. Many libraries rely on that.

In Vapor, there are no VNodes. A slot function returns a block: real DOM nodes wired to reactive effects. The Vue 3.6 release notes are explicit: calling slots.default() in Vapor is not a safe dry run. It can create blocks and DOM nodes, register effects, and claim SSR DOM during hydration.

The VDOM habit that breaks

<!-- ❌ BaseCard.vue: "does the default slot have content?" -->
<script setup vapor>
import { useSlots, computed } from 'vue'

const slots = useSlots()
const isEmpty = computed(() => !slots.default?.()?.length)   // renders the slot!
</script>
<template>
  <div class="card">
    <slot v-if="!isEmpty" />
    <p v-else class="muted">Nothing here yet</p>
  </div>
</template>

What goes wrong, step by step:

  1. computed calls slots.default(). In Vapor this builds the slot's DOM and effects once, just to measure it.
  2. <slot /> in the template renders the slot again. Now you have two sets of effects for the same content, and the first set is not attached anywhere sensible.
  3. During SSR hydration, the first call can adopt the server’s slot HTML. When <slot /> later looks for its nodes, the cursor has already moved past them, and you get a hydration mismatch that looks unrelated to slots.
  4. In VDOM the result is also unreliable: a slot that renders only a v-if="false" comment still returns one VNode, so length is not "empty" anyway.

The fix: let the template own fallback content

<!-- ✅ BaseCard.vue -->
<template vapor>
  <div class="card">
    <slot>
      <p class="muted">Nothing here yet</p>   <!-- fallback content -->
    </slot>
  </div>
</template>

Content between <slot> and </slot> is fallback content. Vue renders it only when the parent provides nothing for that slot. Vue decides this internally, in one place, so the slot renders exactly once.

If you only need to know whether a parent passed a slot at all (for example to skip a wrapper element), check for the slot function without calling it:

<script setup vapor>
import { useSlots } from 'vue'
const slots = useSlots()
</script>

<template>
  <header v-if="slots.header" class="card-header">  <!-- presence check, no call -->
    <slot name="header" />
  </header>
</template>

The difference is subtle but important: slots.header reads a property, while slots.header() runs the slot.

Slots that cross the boundary

Now the boundary-specific part. Slot content always belongs to the component that wrote it, even when another component renders it. When a Vapor parent passes a slot to a VDOM child (or the reverse), the interop layer wraps the slot function so the other engine can call it.

Case 1: Vapor parent, VDOM child with a normal template. The child’s <slot /> compiles to Vue's renderSlot helper, which the interop layer understands. This is the well-tested direction.

Case 2: Vapor parent, VDOM child written as a render function or JSX. Many UI libraries are written this way, and many call slots.default() directly. Vuetify0's Vapor guide notes that interop is directional, and that passing Vapor slots into a VDOM component needs renderSlot rather than slots.default(). If you own the component, update it:

// ✅ A VDOM render-function component that is safe for Vapor slots
import { h, renderSlot } from 'vue'

export default {
  name: 'Panel',
  setup(_, { slots }) {
    return () =>
      h('div', { class: 'panel' }, [
        // instead of: slots.default?.()
        renderSlot(slots, 'default', {}, () => [h('p', 'Empty')]),
      ])
  },
}

renderSlot(slots, name, props, fallback) lets Vue handle the slot through its normal path, including the fallback, instead of your code calling the function directly.

Case 3: forwarded slots. A wrapper that passes its own slot through to an inner component is very common:

<!-- FieldWrapper.vue (VDOM) forwards a slot to a Vapor input -->
<template>
  <VaporInput>
    <template #label><slot name="label">Default label</slot></template>
  </VaporInput>
</template>

This is legal, but forwarded slots with fallbacks are exactly what one of the hydration fixes in rc.1 addressed (“avoid resolving inherited fallback in forwarded slots”). If a forwarded slot shows its fallback when it should not, or the reverse, check this pattern first and upgrade to the latest RC.

Case 4: a component whose root is just <slot />. In rc.9, Vapor started warning when you put a directive on such a component, and v-show on a slot-outlet root is ignored, matching VDOM. If you wrote <Wrapper v-show="open"> where Wrapper's template is only <slot />, move v-show onto a real element.

Good news: provide/inject now flows through slots across the seam. A fix in 3.6.0-alpha.7 enabled injection from a VDOM parent into a slotted Vapor child, so a theme or form context provided above still reaches slotted content.

Gotcha 3: KeepAlive caches two different kinds of things

A <KeepAlive> written in a Vapor template becomes a Vapor-specific KeepAlive, and it caches a Vapor child and a VDOM child in two different ways. Most KeepAlive surprises at the boundary come from that difference.

KeepAlive in one paragraph

Normally, when you switch from one component to another (tabs, wizard steps, routes), Vue unmounts the old one and its state is lost. <KeepAlive> keeps the old component in memory instead. Switching back restores it with its state, scroll position and form inputs intact. Two lifecycle hooks tell the component what happened: onDeactivated when it is put into the cache and onActivated when it comes back.

What changes in 3.6

The pull request that brought KeepAlive to Vapor describes the design clearly:

  • Inside a Vapor component, <KeepAlive> is compiled into VaporKeepAlive.
  • For a Vapor child, VaporKeepAlive caches the component instance.
  • For a VDOM child, it caches the interop fragment that wraps the VDOM tree.
  • The classic VDOM <KeepAlive> can now render and cache Vapor children too.

So all four combinations work. But “cache an instance” and “cache a wrapped fragment” are different mechanisms, and that is where edge cases appear.

A realistic mixed example

A dashboard is converted to Vapor, but the Reports tab still uses a chart library that only ships VDOM components.

<!-- Dashboard.vue -->
<script setup vapor>
import { shallowRef } from 'vue'
import OverviewTab from './OverviewTab.vue'   // <script setup vapor>
import ReportsTab from './ReportsTab.vue'     // VDOM (chart library inside)
import SettingsTab from './SettingsTab.vue'   // <script setup vapor>

const tabs = { overview: OverviewTab, reports: ReportsTab, settings: SettingsTab }
const current = shallowRef('overview')
</script>
<template>
  <nav class="tabs">
    <button v-for="(_, name) in tabs" :key="name" @click="current = name">
      {{ name }}
    </button>
  </nav>
  <!-- Compiled into VaporKeepAlive because this template is Vapor -->
  <KeepAlive :include="['OverviewTab', 'ReportsTab']" :max="5">
    <component :is="tabs[current]" :key="current" />
  </KeepAlive>
</template>

Reading the code line by line:

  1. shallowRef holds the active tab name. We store names, not component objects, in reactive state, which avoids making component definitions deeply reactive.
  2. <component :is> picks which component to render. Because Dashboard is Vapor, this dynamic component and the <KeepAlive> around it are compiled to their Vapor versions.
  3. include lists component names to cache. With <script setup>, the name is inferred from the file name, so OverviewTab.vue is OverviewTab. SettingsTab is not listed, so it is recreated each time.
  4. :key="current" gives each cached entry a stable identity. A 2026 change to the Vapor runtime added tests for KeepAlive cache key resolution and for propagating keys across the VDOM interop layer, so explicit keys are now respected on both sides. Be explicit anyway; it makes the cache predictable.
  5. :max="5" limits memory. When the cache is full, the least recently used entry is destroyed.

At runtime, OverviewTab is cached as a Vapor instance. ReportsTab crosses the boundary, so what gets cached is the interop fragment containing its VDOM tree.

Gotcha 3a: stale or leaking props on a cached VDOM child

While a cached component sits in the cache, its parent may keep changing the props it would receive. In rc.9 the Vue team fixed a case where a cached VDOM child inside a Vapor KeepAlive did not have its props isolated properly. If a hidden VDOM tab seems to react to props meant for the visible one, or shows stale values when re-activated, upgrade to rc.9 or later first. As a defensive habit, pass tabs only the props they actually need, and re-read anything time-sensitive in onActivated.

Gotcha 3b: changing include / exclude at runtime

<script setup vapor>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const cached = ref(['OverviewTab'])
function pinReports() {
  cached.value = [...cached.value, 'ReportsTab']  // changes include while active
}
</script>

<template>
  <KeepAlive :include="cached">
    <component :is="tabs[current]" :key="current" />
  </KeepAlive>
</template>

This is a legitimate feature (“let the user pin a tab”). Before rc.9, Vapor KeepAlive did not cache the currently shown branch when include/exclude changed, so the pinned tab could still be lost on the next switch. The fix landed in rc.9 ("cache current KeepAlive branch when include/exclude changes"). On older RCs, prefer a static include list.

Gotcha 3c: template refs to cached components

A very common VDOM trick is saving scroll position through a component ref:

// ❌ Works in VDOM, not with a Vapor child
const tabRef = ref()
onDeactivated(() => { saved = tabRef.value.$el.scrollTop })

Template refs to Vapor components do not expose $el, $props, $attrs, $slots or $refs. Move the contract into the child itself:

<!-- ✅ ReportsList.vue (Vapor) remembers its own scroll position -->
<script setup vapor>
import { ref, onActivated, onDeactivated } from 'vue'
const listEl = ref(null)          // ref to a real element, not a component
let savedTop = 0
onDeactivated(() => { savedTop = listEl.value?.scrollTop ?? 0 })
onActivated(() => { if (listEl.value) listEl.value.scrollTop = savedTop })
defineExpose({ scrollToTop: () => listEl.value?.scrollTo({ top: 0 }) })
</script>
<template>
  <ul ref="listEl" class="list">
    <slot />
  </ul>
</template>

Why this is better: a ref on a plain <ul> is a real DOM element in both engines. The component remembers its own scroll position through the KeepAlive hooks, and if a parent really needs to control it, defineExpose publishes an explicit method. Parents no longer depend on internals like $el, which do not exist in Vapor.

Gotcha 3d: nested branches inside cached components

Another rc.9 fix covered a KeepAlive component reactivated inside a nested branch (for example a cached tab inside a v-if section that itself toggles) not unmounting correctly. If a tab's onUnmounted never runs, or its effects keep firing after the section closes, look for KeepAlive nested inside conditional branches and upgrade.

A simple rule for KeepAlive at the boundary

Where possible, keep all children of one KeepAlive in the same rendering mode. If one tab must stay VDOM, consider making the KeepAlive’s parent VDOM too, so the classic, battle-tested KeepAlive manages everything, and convert the tabs to Vapor one by one later.

Bonus gotchas you will meet at the seam

Three smaller differences are not about hydration, slots or KeepAlive, but they surface at the same boundary and are easy to mistake for one of them.

Delegated events and a VDOM parent that calls stopPropagation()

Vapor attaches many common events (like click) through one shared listener on document, instead of one listener per element. This is called event delegation, and it saves memory. The catch: a delegated handler only runs when the event bubbles all the way up to document.

<!-- ModalShell.vue (VDOM) -->
<template>
  <div class="modal" @click.stop>   <!-- stops bubbling here -->
    <slot />
  </div>
</template>
<!-- SaveButton.vue (Vapor), rendered inside ModalShell -->
<template vapor>
  <button @click="save">Save</button>   <!-- delegated: never fires! -->
</template>

Why it fails silently: the click starts at the button and bubbles up. ModalShell stops it at .modal, so it never reaches document, where Vapor's shared listener was waiting. No error appears; the button just does nothing.

The 3.6 release notes list three forms that attach the listener directly to the element and bypass delegation:

<button v-on="{ click: save }">Save</button>
<button v-bind="{ onClick: save }">Save</button>
<button @[eventName]="save">Save</button>

The Vue docs team used the first form in their own site for exactly this reason. A cleaner long-term fix is to remove .stop from the ancestor and close the modal by checking event.target === event.currentTarget instead.

getCurrentInstance() returns null in Vapor

Some libraries (and some of our own composables) reach into the current component instance to read proxy, appContext or global properties. In a Vapor component, getCurrentInstance() returns null, and app.config.globalProperties is not supported.

// ❌ Breaks inside a Vapor component
export function useToast() {
  const { proxy } = getCurrentInstance()      // TypeError: null
  return proxy.$toast
}
// ✅ Works in both engines: provide/inject
// plugins/toast.js
export const ToastKey = Symbol('toast')
export default { install(app) { app.provide(ToastKey, createToast()) } }

// composables/useToast.js
import { inject } from 'vue'
import { ToastKey } from '../plugins/toast'
export const useToast = () => inject(ToastKey)

inject() walks up the component tree regardless of which engine rendered each level, so it is the safest way to share services across a boundary.

The rest of the “not in Vapor” list

The release notes also list these as unsupported or not applicable inside Vapor components. If a component relies on one, keep it VDOM for now:

  • Options API (data, methods, mounted, ...)
  • Per-element @vue:mounted style lifecycle events (use a template ref plus onMounted)
  • v-memo
  • Custom directives use a new signature: (node, valueGetter, argument, modifiers), optionally returning a cleanup function. The rc.9 changelog also added a warning for VDOM-style object directives used in Vapor templates.
// ✅ A Vapor-style custom directive
import { watchEffect } from 'vue'

export const vAutofocus = (el, value) => {
  watchEffect(() => { if (value()) el.focus() })   // value is a getter
}

A pre-flight checklist before you add vapor to a component

Run through this list for every component you convert. Each item maps to one of the gotchas above, so a “no” tells you exactly which section to reread.

Is the component eligible?

  • It uses <script setup> or is template-only (no Options API).
  • It does not call getCurrentInstance() or read globalProperties, directly or through a composable.
  • It does not use v-memo or @vue: element lifecycle events.

Where will the boundary be?

  • The boundary sits above any v-for, not inside it.
  • The component’s parent and children are mostly in the same mode, or you have a reason for each crossing.
  • A component sitting directly on the boundary has a single root element.

Hydration (SSR only)

  • The first render uses no client-only values (time, window, random, locale).
  • The root element is valid where it is placed (no block element inside <p>, <a>, <button>).
  • You tested a hard refresh of the page with __VUE_PROD_HYDRATION_MISMATCH_DETAILS__ on.

Slots

  • No code calls slots.xxx() just to check content. Fallbacks live inside <slot>...</slot>.
  • Any VDOM render-function component receiving its slots uses renderSlot.
  • Forwarded slots with fallbacks are tested on the latest RC.

KeepAlive

  • Children of one <KeepAlive> share a rendering mode, or you tested the mixed case.
  • Dynamic components inside it have explicit :keys.
  • No parent reads $el or $refs from a cached Vapor child.

Events

  • No VDOM ancestor calls stopPropagation() on events a Vapor child needs, or the child binds them with v-on="{ click: fn }".

If you prefer a visual version, the flowchart below asks the same questions in order and tells you whether to convert a component now, wrap it, or leave it on VDOM for this release.

Wrapping up

Vapor Mode is the biggest change to how Vue renders since Vue 3 itself, and the 3.6 RCs make it practical to adopt one page at a time. The price of incremental adoption is the boundary: two engines that must agree on the same HTML, the same slot functions and the same cache.

If you remember only three things from this article, make them these:

  1. Hydration: render the same structure on server and client, and only change client-only values after onMounted.
  2. Slots: never call a slot to inspect it. Let <slot> fallbacks and renderSlot decide.
  3. KeepAlive: keep each KeepAlive’s children in one rendering mode, give them keys, and never reach into a cached Vapor child through $el.

And above all: draw your boundaries deliberately, as few and as high in the tree as you can. Pin an exact RC, read the minor branch changelog before each bump, and measure before and after on a real page.

Have you tried Vapor on a production-like page yet? I would love to hear which boundary bit you first. Share it in the comments.

import type { H3Event } from "h3";
import {
  serverSupabaseUser,
  serverSupabaseServiceRole,

} from "#supabase/server";

export async function requireAdmin(event: H3Event) {
  const claims = await serverSupabaseUser(event);

  const adminId = claims?.sub;
  if (!adminId) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 401, statusMessage: "Unauthorized" });
  }

  const admin = serverSupabaseServiceRole<any>(event);
  const { data, error } = await admin
    .from("users")
    .select("role")
    .eq("id", adminId)
    .single();

  if (error || data?.role !== "admin") {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404, statusMessage: "Not Found" });
  }

  return { adminId, admin };
}

import type { H3Event } from "h3";
const UUID_RE = /^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/i;

export function requireUuidParam(event: H3Event, name = "id") {
  const value = getRouterParam(event, name);
  if (!value || !UUID_RE.test(value)) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 400, statusMessage: "Invalid id" });
  }
  return value;
}

Bikin file index.post.ts di dalam folder server/api/users, lalu isi file tsb dengan code:

import { storeUserSchema } from "~~/shared/utils/userSchema";

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const { admin } = await requireAdmin(event);

  const body = await readValidatedBody(event, storeUserSchema.parse);

  // 1. Buat akun di Supabase Auth
  const { data: created, error: authError } = await admin.auth.admin.createUser({
    email: body.email,
    password: body.password,
    email_confirm: true,
    user_metadata: { name: body.name },
  });

  if (authError || !created.user) {
    const exists = authError?.code === "email_exists";
    throw createError({
      statusCode: exists ? 409 : 500,
      statusMessage: exists
        ? "Email already registered"
        : (authError?.message ?? "Failed to create user"),
    });
  }

  // 2. Isi baris profil. Upsert, jaga-jaga kalau ada trigger yang sudah membuatnya
  const { data: user, error: insertError } = await admin
    .from("users")
    .upsert(
      {
        id: created.user.id,
        name: body.name,
        email: body.email,
        role: body.role,
      },
      { onConflict: "id" },
    )
    .select("id, name, email, role, created_at")
    .single();

  if (insertError) {
    // rollback supaya tidak ada akun yatim di Authentication
    await admin.auth.admin.deleteUser(created.user.id);
    throw createError({ statusCode: 500, statusMessage: insertError.message });
  }

  return user;
});

7.4. UPDATE USER

Bikin file [id].put.ts di dalam folder server/api/users, lalu isi file tsb dengan code:

import { requireUuidParam } from "~~/server/utils/requireUuidParam";
import { updateUserSchema } from "~~/shared/utils/userSchema";

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const { adminId, admin } = await requireAdmin(event);
  const id = requireUuidParam(event);

  const { name, email, password, role } = await readValidatedBody(
    event,
    updateUserSchema.parse,
  );

  // Cegah admin mengunci dirinya sendiri
  if (id === adminId && role && role !== "admin") {
    throw createError({
      statusCode: 400,
      statusMessage: "You cannot remove your own admin role",
    });
  }

  const { data: existing, error: findError } = await admin
    .from("users")
    .select("id")
    .eq("id", id)
    .maybeSingle();

  if (findError) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 500, statusMessage: findError.message });
  }
  if (!existing) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404, statusMessage: "User not found" });
  }

  // 1. Akun Auth: email, password, nama
  if (name || email || password) {
    const { error: authError } = await admin.auth.admin.updateUserById(id, {
      ...(email && { email, email_confirm: true }),
      ...(password && { password }),
      ...(name && { user_metadata: { name } }),
    });

    if (authError) {
      const exists = authError.code === "email_exists";
      throw createError({
        statusCode: exists ? 409 : 500,
        statusMessage: exists ? "Email already registered" : authError.message,
      });
    }
  }

  // 2. Baris profil: hanya kolom yang dikirim
  const patch = {
    ...(name && { name }),
    ...(email && { email }),
    ...(role && { role }),
  };

  if (Object.keys(patch).length > 0) {
    const { error } = await admin.from("users").update(patch).eq("id", id);
    if (error) {
      throw createError({ statusCode: 500, statusMessage: error.message });
    }
  }

  const { data: user, error: readError } = await admin
    .from("users")
    .select("id, name, email, role, created_at")
    .eq("id", id)
    .single();

  if (readError) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 500, statusMessage: readError.message });
  }

  return user;
});

7.5. DELETE USER

Bikin file [id].delete.ts di dalam folder server/api/users, lalu isi file tsb dengan code:

import { requireUuidParam } from "~~/server/utils/requireUuidParam";

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const { adminId, admin } = await requireAdmin(event);

  const id = requireUuidParam(event);

  if (id === adminId) {
    throw createError({
      statusCode: 400,
      statusMessage: "Cannot delete your own account",
    });
  }

  // 1. Hapus baris profil (service role, tidak kena RLS)
  const { data, error } = await admin
    .from("users")
    .delete()
    .eq("id", id)
    .select("id");

  if (error) {
    const inUse = error.code === "23503"; // masih dipakai tabel lain
    throw createError({
      statusCode: inUse ? 409 : 500,
      statusMessage: inUse ? "User is still referenced by other data" : error.message,
    });
  }

  // 2. Hapus akun di Supabase Auth
  const { error: authError } = await admin.auth.admin.deleteUser(id);
  if (authError && authError.code !== "user_not_found") {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 500, statusMessage: authError.message });
  }

  // Tidak ada yang terhapus di kedua tempat: jangan pura-pura sukses
  if (data.length === 0 && authError?.code === "user_not_found") {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404, statusMessage: "User not found" });
  }

  return { deleted: true };
});

        method: "post",
        body: createForm,
      });

      toast.add({
        title: "Success: User Created",
        color: "success",
        id: "modal-success",
      });
      await navigateTo("/admin/users");
    } catch (error: any) {
      toast.add({
        title: `Fail: ${getErrorMessage(error)}`,
        color: "error",
        id: "modal-dismiss",
      });
    }
  };

  const editUser = async ({
    id,
    updateForm,
  }: {
    id: string | undefined;
    updateForm: UpdateUserData;
  }) => {
    if (!id) return;

    try {
      await $fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, {
        method: "PUT",
        body: updateForm,
      });

      toast.add({
        title: "Success: User Updated",
        color: "success",
        id: "modal-success",
      });
      await navigateTo("/admin/users");
    } catch (error: any) {
      toast.add({
        title: `Fail: ${getErrorMessage(error)}`,
        color: "error",
        id: "modal-dismiss",
      });
    }
  };

  async function deleteUser({
    name,
    id,
    refreshAction,
  }: {
    name: string;
    id: string;
    refreshAction: () => void;
  }) {
    const instance = modal.open({
      title: `Delete ${name}'s User`,
      description: `Are you sure you want to delete ${name}'s user?`,
    });
    const isDeleteValid = await instance.result;

    if (!isDeleteValid) {
      toast.add({
        title: "Delete the user cancelled",
        color: "neutral",
        id: "modal-dismiss",
      });
      return;
    }

    try {
      await $fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { method: "DELETE" });
      refreshAction();

      toast.add({
        title: "Successfully delete the user",
        color: "success",
        id: "modal-success",
      });
    } catch (error: any) {
      toast.add({
        title: `Fail: ${getErrorMessage(error)}`,
        color: "error",
        id: "modal-dismiss",
      });
    }
  }

  return { createForm,createUser ,editUser, deleteUser };
};

corrida_no_ar.titulo: Maratona do Rio conquista SELO GOLD e PREMIAÇÃO RECORDE em 2027
corrida_no_ar.resumo: A Maratona do Rio conquista o Selo Gold para 2027 e anuncia premiação recorde, mas comete erros em seu comunicado. Veja também a elite da Maratona de Maringá, a nova campanha da São Silvestre e a investigação do Ministério Público sobre a Meia de João Pessoa.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 19 de novembro de 2026

A Maratona do Rio de Janeiro conquistou o Selo Gold da World Athletics para a sua prova de 42 km em 2027. Com a chancela, a prova avança de categoria e terá uma premiação recorde de quase R$ 2 milhões, com valores iguais para homens e mulheres.

No entanto, o comunicado oficial da prova, divulgado à imprensa, continha dois erros importantes. O primeiro afirmava que a prova seria a “única maratona da América Latina com a certificação” em 2027. Isso não é verdade: a Maratona da Cidade do México já possui o Selo Gold desde 2023. O segundo erro foi dizer que o evento reuniu “cerca de 70 mil corredores” em 2026. Esse número se refere ao total de vagas oferecidas, e não ao número de participantes. Dados oficiais mostram que 57.792 pessoas concluíram as provas do festival em 2026.

Apesar das incorreções, a notícia é fantástica para a corrida no Brasil. A premiação total para a maratona em 2027 será de US$ 374 mil, um aumento de 38,5% em relação a 2026. Os campeões masculino e feminino levarão para casa US$ 90 mil cada, o equivalente a cerca de R$ 488 mil. A prova, que em 2026 recebeu o selo Elite, dá um passo importante para se consolidar no cenário internacional e, quem sabe, buscar o selo Platinum no futuro.

Segundo João Traven, sócio-fundador da Maratona do Rio, o Selo Gold é resultado de um trabalho que vai além do dia da corrida, envolvendo planejamento, investimento na elite e qualidade do percurso. Duda Magalhães, presidente da Dream Factory, que organiza o evento, completou: “O Gold Label fortalece essa estratégia porque acrescenta credibilidade esportiva a um evento que já tem escala, história e uma cidade com enorme capacidade de atração.”

Divulgada a elite da Maratona de Maringá

A Maratona Internacional de Maringá, que acontece no próximo domingo e já possui o Permit Ouro da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt), divulgou a sua lista de atletas de elite para as provas de 42 km e 21 km.

Na maratona masculina, os destaques brasileiros são Franck Caldeira, Gilberto Silvestre Lopes, Givaldo Araújo de Sena, José Marcio Leão e Samuel do Nascimento. Entre os estrangeiros, estão Adguna Gadisa Ashenafi (Etiópia), Jonathan Akankwasa (Uganda) e Justin Mose Mogire (Quênia). No feminino, o pelotão conta com as brasileiras Adriana Domingos da Silva, Aline Barbosa dos Santos, Eulália dos Santos e Rosângela Vieira, além das etíopes Desta Abera Demise e Zewudnesh Hurisa Degofa, e das quenianas Purity Kagendo Knjy, Vivian Jeftanui Kiplagati e Vivian Jelagat Jeptopkeny.

Na meia maratona, os nomes fortes no masculino são Damião Ancelmo de Souza, Daniel Nascimento, Edson Emídio e Miguel Morone Neto. No feminino, a disputa terá Amanda Aparecida de Oliveira, a queniana Naum Jepchirchir e Tatiane Raquel da Silva. O Corrida no Ar fará a transmissão ao vivo da prova.

São Silvestre lança campanha para corredores

A organização da Corrida Internacional de São Silvestre anunciou uma nova campanha. A ação dará a corredores anônimos a chance de “ser a estrela da campanha” da 101ª edição da prova. A organização afirmou que em breve revelará em suas redes sociais como os interessados poderão fazer parte desse “momento histórico”.

MP da Paraíba investiga falhas na Meia de João Pessoa

O Ministério Público da Paraíba (MPPB) instaurou um procedimento para apurar falhas na organização da Meia Maratona de João Pessoa, realizada no último fim de semana. A investigação foi iniciada após o órgão receber denúncias de falta de água nos postos de hidratação, o que teria causado desmaios entre os participantes.

O 44º promotor de Justiça de João Pessoa, Adrio Nobre Leite, que atua na defesa do consumidor, está à frente do caso. O MP deu um prazo de 15 dias para que a organização do evento, a Federação Paraibana de Atletismo e a Secretaria de Saúde da capital prestem informações sobre o ocorrido. A falha na hidratação teria afetado principalmente corredores amadores e iniciantes.
